title: Newly discovered mechanism protects DNA during cell division
excerpt: Every time a cell divides, it must accurately copy and distribute its DNA between two new cells. However, in some cases, chromosomes do not fully separate, leaving behind thin strands of DNA known as DNA bridges that connect the two newly formed cells.
content_html:
Every time a cell divides, it must accurately copy and distribute its DNA between two new cells. However, in some cases, chromosomes do not fully separate, leaving behind thin strands of DNA known as DNA bridges that connect the two newly formed cells.

These fragile structures can be vulnerable to damage and, if not properly managed, can have severe consequences for genome stability. Researchers from King's, in collaboration with research teams at the University of Utah and biotechnology company Altos Labs, have now revealed how cells protect themselves from this threat.

Published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, the study shows that ESCRT-III proteins, previously known for helping cells reshape and repair membranes, have an unexpected role in protecting DNA bridges during cell division.

A checkpoint buys time for protection

During cell division, a safety mechanism called the NoCut checkpoint helps delay the final stages of division when DNA bridges are present. The researchers found that this delay allows ESCRT-III proteins to move to the DNA bridges, where they form a protective coating around the exposed DNA and help prevent damage.

Although DNA bridges are rare in healthy cells, research has linked them to genome instability and some early events associated with cancer development. While the study does not directly demonstrate a link between this mechanism and cancer development, it provides new insight into how cells protect themselves from DNA damage events that have previously been associated with genome instability and disease.

Juan Martin-Serrano, professor of viral cell biology at King's and co-senior author of the study, said, "The discovery came from an unexpected observation. We saw ESCRT proteins binding to DNA but didn't understand why. After more than 20 years studying these proteins, I never imagined we would uncover this completely new role for them. There is still much more to understand, and our next steps will be to investigate how these DNA bridges form and what enables them to protect the genome."

How the team captured it

To study these events at the molecular level, the team used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of the ESCRT/DNA complex. Advanced live-cell microscopy allowed them to watch cells divide in real time. Researchers created specialized cell lines containing fluorescently labeled proteins, enabling them to track DNA and ESCRT proteins as they moved inside living cells.

Because DNA bridges occur infrequently, the researchers used two approaches to study them. They first analyzed large numbers of cells to identify naturally occurring DNA bridges. They also temporarily blocked the activity of a protein involved in separating DNA during cell division, increasing the number of DNA bridges available for detailed analysis.

Dr. James Glover, co-first author of the study, completed his undergraduate degree, master's and Ph.D. at King's, with his doctoral research carried out in Martin-Serrano's laboratory through the Medical Research Council Doctoral Training Partnership (MRC DTP). He is now continuing his research career internationally as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Berkeley.

An unexpected role for ESCRT

Reflecting on the significance of the discovery, Glover said, "When we think about cell division, we often imagine the textbook picture of one cell dividing into two cells with DNA being perfectly distributed. But in reality, many complications can happen as those cells separate.

"What we've discovered is that ESCRT proteins can come in and protect DNA bridges, preventing them from causing damage. The fact that a family of proteins known for remodeling membranes can also protect DNA is such an unexpected and exciting discovery."

Publication details

James Glover et al, ESCRT-III assembles around mis-segregated DNA to protect genome stability, Nature Structural & Molecular Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41594-026-01841-4

content_html_zh:
每次细胞分裂时，它都必须在两个新细胞之间准确地复制和分配其 DNA。 然而，在某些情况下，染色体不会完全分离，留下称为 DNA 桥的细 DNA 链，连接两个新形成的细胞。

这些脆弱的结构很容易受到损坏，如果管理不当，可能会对基因组稳定性产生严重后果。 国王学院的研究人员与犹他大学和生物技术公司 Altos Labs 的研究团队合作，现已揭示了细胞如何保护自己免受这种威胁。

该研究发表在《自然结构与分子生物学》上，表明 ESCRT-III 蛋白以前以帮助细胞重塑和修复细胞膜而闻名，但在细胞分裂过程中保护 DNA 桥方面具有意想不到的作用。

检查站为保护赢得时间

在细胞分裂过程中，当 DNA 桥存在时，一种称为 NoCut 检查点的安全机制有助于延迟分裂的最后阶段。 研究人员发现，这种延迟使得 ESCRT-III 蛋白能够移动到 DNA 桥，在暴露的 DNA 周围形成保护层，有助于防止损伤。

尽管 DNA 桥在健康细胞中很少见，但研究已将其与基因组不稳定和一些与癌症发展相关的早期事件联系起来。 虽然该研究没有直接证明这种机制与癌症发展之间的联系，但它提供了关于细胞如何保护自身免受先前与基因组不稳定和疾病相关的 DNA 损伤事件的新见解。

国王学院病毒细胞生物学教授、该研究的共同高级作者胡安·马丁-塞拉诺说：“这一发现来自一次意想不到的观察。 我们看到 ESCRT 蛋白与 DNA 结合，但不明白为什么。 经过 20 多年的研究这些蛋白质，我从未想过我们会发现它们的这种全新作用。 还有很多东西需要了解，我们下一步将研究这些 DNA 桥是如何形成的，以及是什么使它们能够保护基因组。”

团队如何捕捉它

为了在分子水平上研究这些事件，研究小组使用冷冻电子显微镜来确定 ESCRT/DNA 复合物的结构。 先进的活细胞显微镜使他们能够实时观察细胞分裂。 研究人员创建了含有荧光标记蛋白质的特殊细胞系，使它们能够在 DNA 和 ESCRT 蛋白质在活细胞内移动时对其进行追踪。

由于 DNA 桥很少出现，研究人员使用了两种方法来研究它们。 他们首先分析了大量细胞来识别自然存在的 DNA 桥。 他们还暂时阻断了细胞分裂过程中参与分离 DNA 的蛋白质的活性，增加了可用于详细分析的 DNA 桥的数量。

该研究的共同第一作者 James Glover 博士完成了本科、硕士和博士学位。 他在国王学院获得博士学位，并通过医学研究委员会博士培训合作伙伴关系 (MRC DTP) 在 Martin-Serrano 实验室进行了博士研究。 他目前在加州大学伯克利分校担任博士后研究员，继续他的国际研究生涯。

ESRT 的意想不到的作用

谈及这一发现的意义时，格洛弗说：“当我们思考细胞分裂时，我们经常会想象教科书上的画面：一个细胞分裂成两个细胞，并且 DNA 分布完美。 但实际上，当这些细胞分离时，可能会发生许多并发症。

“我们发现 ESCRT 蛋白可以进入并保护 DNA 桥，防止它们造成损害。 事实上，一类以重塑膜而闻名的蛋白质也可以保护 DNA，这是一个意想不到且令人兴奋的发现。”
